unit-phys-conv.title: Kinematics 1 · Unit Conversions
unit-phys-conv.srcName: HW03 Unit Conversion + Unusual Conversion Factors (Drive)

summary.text: Unit conversions the way physicists actually do them: the factor-label method (multiply by fractions equal to 1 until the units you don't want cancel). Covers the class conversion table — stones, rods, chains, furlongs, leagues, acres, knots — plus the cross conversions like mi/hr to m/s where BOTH top and bottom units change.

why.text: Every kinematics problem this year starts by getting the units right — a speed in furlongs per fortnight is useless until it is meters per second. The factor-label method is one procedure that solves every conversion, no matter how weird the units. Master the setup and the arithmetic is just multiplication.

objectives.text: Set up any conversion as a chain of unit fractions, cancelling units diagonally until only the target unit survives.
Use the class conversion table: stone, rod, chain, furlong, league, acre, knot, and the metric bridges (1 in = 2.54 cm, 1 kg = 2.2 lb).
Do cross conversions where numerator AND denominator both change — mi/hr to m/s, leagues/min to km/hr.
Handle squared and cubed units: converting ft² or (acre)(ft) means the factor gets squared or applied per dimension.

parentNote.text: Built for Monday's quiz from the two Kinematics 1 documents in Drive: the Unusual Conversion Factors table (all factors below are that sheet's, verbatim) and the HW03 problem types (imperial one-step chains, then cross conversions). Every problem here is FRESH — HW03 stays her homework, per the house rules — but the shapes match: same table, same skills, similar magnitudes. Every answer was re-derived independently; the walkthroughs teach the factor-label setup one cancellation at a time, which is what 'show your work to earn credit' means on her homework. The trap to watch: squared units (an acre is 43560 ft², so ft²→chains² needs the 66-ft factor used twice).

nextUp.text: Cards once, then quiz rounds until the setups feel automatic. The calculator is right there in the quiz — the method is the skill, not the arithmetic.

cards.def:
**Multiply by conversion fractions equal to 1, arranged so unwanted units cancel diagonally.**
• Each fraction is a true equation written as a fraction: 5280 ft / 1 mi is just the number 1 wearing units.
• Put the unit you want to KILL on the opposite side of the fraction from where it currently is.
• When only the target unit survives, multiply the numbers.
cards.hint: You are never changing the amount — only multiplying by 1, over and over.

cards.def:
**The setup IS the physics — the arithmetic is just the last step.**
• A written chain of fractions proves the units cancel; an answer alone proves nothing.
• The homework says it plainly: no work, no credit.
cards.hint: Write the fractions first. The calculator finishes; it never starts.

cards.def:
**86 400 sec = 1 day; 3600 sec = 1 hr; 60 sec = 1 min.**
• 86 400 is on the class sheet — it is 24 × 3600, worth checking once so you trust it forever.
cards.hint: A day is about 10⁵ seconds — a handy sanity check.

cards.def:
**5280 ft = 1 mile, and the odd ones are all defined in feet:**
• 1 rod = 16.5 ft
• 1 chain = 66 ft (four rods)
• 1 furlong = 660 ft (ten chains)
• 1 league = 18 228 ft
cards.hint: Rod → chain → furlong: each is a neat multiple of the last (×4, ×10).

cards.def:
**1 in = 2.54 cm — the exact door between imperial and metric.**
• Any length cross-over can route through it: ft → in → cm → m.
• Memorize this one; everything else can be rebuilt from it.
cards.hint: 2.54 is exact by definition — not a rounded number.

cards.def:
**1 kg = 2.2 lb and 1 stone = 14 lb.**
• Stones are a British body-weight unit — 72 lb is a little over 5 stones.
• kg ↔ lb is the metric bridge for mass on the class sheet.
cards.hint: Stone: think 14 — two weeks of pounds.

cards.def:
**1 acre = 43 560 ft² — an AREA, so any conversion out of acres deals in squared lengths.**
• Acres → chains²: divide by 66² ft² per chain², and 43 560 / 4356 = exactly 10 chains².
• An (acre)(ft) is a VOLUME: area × depth, used for water.
cards.hint: 43 560 = 66² × 10 — the acre is secretly ten square chains.

cards.def:
**1 gallon = 128 ounces = 3.785 liters.**
• Two doors out of gallons: one imperial (ounces), one metric (liters).
cards.hint: A 2-liter soda bottle is about half a gallon — sanity check.

cards.def:
**1 knot = 1.15 mi/hr — a speed unit, so it converts in one step to other speeds.**
• Ships and planes use knots; the factor is already a ratio, no chain needed for mi/hr.
cards.hint: Knots are slightly fast miles per hour.

cards.def:
**When the unit is a fraction (mi/hr), convert top and bottom separately in one chain.**
• mi/hr → m/s: kill miles with feet, feet with inches, inches with cm, cm with m — then kill hours with seconds.
• The classic result: 60 mi/hr ≈ 26.8 m/s.
cards.hint: One chain, two jobs: numerator units and denominator units each get cancelled.

cards.def:
**A squared unit needs the conversion factor squared.**
• ft² → chains²: divide by 66 twice, not once.
• in³ ← ft³: multiply by 12 three times (1728).
• This is the most-missed move on conversion quizzes.
cards.hint: The little ² means the factor goes in twice. No exceptions.

cards.def:
**Before trusting the number, ask: should it be bigger or smaller?**
• Feet → miles: miles are huge, so the number must SHRINK.
• Hours → seconds: seconds are tiny, so the number must GROW.
• If the direction is wrong, the fraction was upside down.
cards.hint: Bigger unit, smaller number. Smaller unit, bigger number. Always.

cards.def:
**Every 'unusual' unit was somebody's ordinary.**
• A furlong is one plow-furrow long; an acre is what an ox team plowed in a day; a chain was a literal surveyor's chain.
• Units are frozen history — and the factor-label method eats them all the same way.
cards.hint: The method doesn't care how weird the unit is. That is the whole point of the method.

questions.q: Set up: convert 9240 ft to miles. Which fraction do you multiply by?
questions.hint: Feet must cancel — so feet goes on the bottom.
steps: You start with feet on top, so the fraction needs feet on the BOTTOM to cancel it.
The true equation is 5280 ft = 1 mi; written with feet down, that is 1 mi / 5280 ft.
9240 ft × (1 mi / 5280 ft) = 1.75 mi. Feet cancel, miles survive — that is the whole method.

ex.main: **1 mi / 5280 ft.** The unit you are killing goes on the opposite side of the fraction. Everything else in this unit is this move, repeated.
ex.tip: Write the units first and cancel them like factors — only then touch the numbers.

questions.q: A trail is 4620 ft long. How many chains is that?
questions.hint: 1 chain = 66 ft, and feet must shrink.
steps: Set up so feet cancel: 4620 ft × (1 chain / 66 ft).
Sanity check: chains are bigger than feet, so the number should shrink — 4620 → 70. It did. Answer: 70 chains.

ex.main: **70 chains.** 4620 ÷ 66 = 70 exactly — the sheet's factors are chosen to divide cleanly more often than you'd expect.
ex.tip: When a division comes out perfectly even, that is usually the sheet telling you the setup was right.

questions.q: A hiker weighs 98 lb. In stones, that is:
questions.hint: 1 stone = 14 lb. Should the number get bigger or smaller?
steps: Stones are bigger than pounds, so the count must shrink — that rules out 1372 immediately.
Set up: 98 lb × (1 stone / 14 lb).
98 / 14 = 7. Answer: 7 stones.

ex.main: **7 stones.** The wrong answers are all setup errors: 1372 is multiplying instead of dividing, 44.5 uses 2.2, 9.8 just moves the decimal.
ex.tip: Each wrong option on a conversion quiz is usually one specific mistake. Learn to name them and you can't be fooled.

questions.hint: 3600 seconds per hour — or notice it is exactly half of 86 400.
steps: Route: seconds → hours needs 3600 sec = 1 hr.
Shortcut check: the class sheet says 86 400 sec = 1 day; 43 200 is half of that — half a day — 12 hours. Two routes, same answer.

ex.main: **12 hours.** When two different factor routes give the same answer, you KNOW it is right — that is the built-in error check of the method.
ex.tip: The 86 400 factor is a day; half-days and quarter-days make fast mental checks.

questions.q: A fence is 24 rods long. In feet:
questions.hint: 1 rod = 16.5 ft, and feet are smaller — the number grows.
steps: Feet are smaller than rods, so the number must GROW: 24 → something bigger. That kills 1.45.
Set up: 24 rods × (16.5 ft / 1 rod).

ex.main: **396 ft.** 24 × 16.5: do it as 24 × 16 + 24 × 0.5 = 384 + 12 = 396 — splitting the multiplication beats reaching for the calculator.
ex.tip: ×16.5 = ×16 + ×half. Ugly factors usually split into friendly pieces.

questions.q: A racetrack is 8 furlongs. How many feet is the full track?
questions.hint: 1 furlong = 660 ft. Eight of them is a familiar number.
steps: Set up: 8 furlongs × (660 ft / 1 furlong).
Recognize it: 5280 ft is exactly one mile — 8 furlongs IS the mile, which is why horse races are measured in furlongs.

ex.main: **5280 ft — exactly a mile.** The old units interlock: 4 rods to the chain, 10 chains to the furlong, 8 furlongs to the mile.
ex.tip: Spotting that an answer equals a famous constant (5280!) is the strongest possible confirmation.

questions.q: Convert 30 mi/hr to m/s (use 1 mi = 5280 ft, 1 ft = 12 in, 1 in = 2.54 cm). Closest answer:
questions.hint: Half of the classic 60 mi/hr ≈ 26.8 m/s.
steps: Chain the numerator: 30 mi × 5280 ft/mi × 12 in/ft × 2.54 cm/in = 4 828 032 cm = 48 280.32 m.
Chain the denominator: 1 hr = 3600 s.
Sanity check: 60 mi/hr ≈ 26.8 m/s is the classic conversion, and 30 is half of 60 — so 13.4 is exactly right.

ex.main: **≈13.4 m/s.** One long chain: miles→feet→inches→cm→m on top, hours→seconds on the bottom. Every factor is on the class sheet or is a factor you already own.
ex.tip: Memorize 60 mi/hr ≈ 27 m/s as an anchor — then scale: half the mph, half the m/s.

questions.q: A ship logs 20 knots. Using 1 knot = 1.15 mi/hr, its speed in mi/hr is:
questions.hint: Knots are already a speed — one factor does it.
steps: The knot factor is already a ratio of speeds, so no chain is needed: 20 knots × (1.15 mi/hr / 1 knot).
Check direction: knots are slightly faster than mi/hr, so the number should grow a little. 20 → 23. Answer: 23 mi/hr.

ex.main: **23 mi/hr.** The trap answer is 17.4 — that is dividing by 1.15, flipping the factor upside down. Direction-check before you commit.
ex.tip: 17.4 vs 23: the sanity check ('knots are faster') settles it without redoing any arithmetic.

questions.q: How many square chains is HALF an acre? (1 acre = 43 560 ft², 1 chain = 66 ft)
questions.hint: First find chains² in a full acre — the 66 gets used twice.
steps: A chain² is 66 ft × 66 ft = 4356 ft² — the factor is SQUARED because the unit is squared.
Full acre: 43 560 ft² × (1 chain² / 4356 ft²) = 10 chains².
Half an acre: 10 / 2 = 5 chains².

ex.main: **5 chains².** The acre is exactly 10 square chains — old surveyors designed it that way. The whole problem hinges on squaring the 66.
ex.tip: See a ² on the unit? The conversion factor goes in twice. This is the most-missed move on every conversions quiz.

questions.q: A pond holds 2 (acre)(ft) of water — 2 acres of surface, 1 foot deep. What kind of quantity is an (acre)(ft)?
opts: A length, because feet are in it
An area, because acres are in it
steps: An acre is an area (ft²); a foot is a length (ft).
Area × length = ft² × ft = ft³ — three lengths multiplied, which is a volume.
That is why water districts measure reservoirs in acre-feet: surface area times depth. Converting it to in³ means converting ft³ with the 12 used three times.

ex.main: **A volume.** Units multiply like numbers: ft² × ft = ft³. Reading the dimension off the units works for any combination you will ever meet.
ex.tip: When a unit looks weird, multiply out its dimensions — the ² and ³ tell you what kind of thing it measures.

questions.q: Which of these fractions is NOT equal to 1?
questions.hint: Each fraction is only 'a 1' if top and bottom are truly equal.
steps: The method only works because each fraction equals 1 — top and bottom must be the same amount in different clothes.
5280 ft is a mile ✓, 14 lb is a stone ✓, a gallon is 3.785 L ✓.
60 sec is a MINUTE, not an hour — that fraction equals 1/60, and multiplying by it silently shrinks the answer. Wrong factor, wrong everything.

ex.main: **60 sec / 1 hr.** One false factor poisons the whole chain — which is why writing the equalities down beats trusting memory.
ex.tip: The most common conversion error isn't arithmetic — it is a factor that was never true.

questions.q: 17.6 lb is how many kilograms? (1 kg = 2.2 lb)
questions.hint: Kilograms are heavier than pounds — fewer of them.
steps: Direction: kg is the bigger unit, so the number must shrink — 38.7 and 80 are out instantly.
Set up: 17.6 lb × (1 kg / 2.2 lb).

ex.main: **8 kg.** Two answers died on the sanity check before any arithmetic happened. That is the check doing its job.
ex.tip: Eliminate by direction first; divide second. Half the options usually never deserve arithmetic.

questions.q: Put the factor-label steps for '3 furlongs → inches' in working order.
opts: Multiply by 660 ft / 1 furlong to reach feet
Multiply by 12 in / 1 ft to reach inches
questions.hint: Have → hop to feet → hop to inches → then arithmetic, last.
steps: Always start by writing the given quantity with its unit: 3 furlongs.
First hop: furlongs die when 660 ft / 1 furlong puts furlongs on the bottom.
Second hop: feet die under 12 in / 1 ft, leaving only inches.
Numbers come LAST: 3 × 660 × 12 = 23 760 inches. Setup first, arithmetic once.

ex.main: **Have → factor → factor → multiply.** The chain is planned entirely in units before a single number is computed — that is what full credit looks like.
ex.tip: If you touch the calculator before the units cancel on paper, you are doing it in the wrong order.

questions.q: Convert 2 leagues/min to km/hr (1 league = 18 228 ft, 1 ft = 12 in, 1 in = 2.54 cm). Closest answer:
questions.hint: Leagues are enormous and minutes are short — expect a huge speed.
steps: Numerator: 2 leagues × 18 228 ft × 12 in/ft × 2.54 cm/in = 1 111 178 cm ≈ 11.11 km.
Denominator: 1 min = 1/60 hr, so per-minute becomes per-hour by MULTIPLYING by 60.
11.11 km/min × 60 min/hr ≈ 667 km/hr.
Sanity: a league is ~3.5 miles; 2 per minute is 7 miles a minute — 420 mi/hr territory — so hundreds of km/hr is the right ballpark.

ex.main: **≈667 km/hr.** The tempting error is dividing by 60 instead of multiplying — but something per MINUTE happens 60 times per HOUR, so per-hour numbers grow.
ex.tip: Per-minute → per-hour always multiplies by 60. If your speed shrank, the time factor went in upside down.

questions.q: A recipe needs 64 ounces of stock. In gallons, that is:
steps: Set up so ounces cancel: 64 oz × (1 gal / 128 oz).
Direction check: gallons are much bigger than ounces, so a small number is expected. Answer: half a gallon.

ex.main: **0.5 gallons.** 8192 is the upside-down setup (×128) — it fails the sniff test instantly, because 64 ounces is obviously not thousands of gallons.
ex.tip: Absurd magnitudes are gifts: any answer that offends common sense was an inverted fraction.

questions.q: Your chain gives an answer in cm but the quiz asks for meters. What is the LAST fraction in the chain?
questions.hint: Centimeters must die — where do they sit in the fraction?
steps: The surviving unit is cm; to kill it, cm goes on the bottom of the final factor.
The true equality is 100 cm = 1 m, written cm-down: 1 m / 100 cm.
Result: the number shrinks by 100 and the unit flips to meters — done.

ex.main: **1 m / 100 cm.** Same rule as every other step: the doomed unit rides the bottom. Metric steps are just powers of ten, which is why the chain usually ends metric.
ex.tip: Finish chains in metric when you can — the last hops become decimal shifts instead of long division.
